title: The Exhaustion of Always Trying to Become Someone

reels.hook: A quiet Sunday. Nothing scheduled. Still tired.
reels.hook_b: The tiredness that sleep doesn't fix.
cards: A quiet Sunday. Nothing scheduled. Still tired.
Learning a language. Fixing your posture. Becoming more present.
Never allowed to just be someone.
Psychologists link the gap between who we are and who we 'should' be to distress.
A self always under construction never closes the gap.
Send it to someone who needs a day off from improving.

reels.caption:
There's a tiredness that comes not from doing too much but from always being in progress.

Self-discrepancy theory links the gap between who we are and who we think we should be to distress. A self that's never finished keeps that gap open forever.

What would you stop improving if you were allowed to?

Theory: Higgins (1987); later studies support the general link, less so the specifics. Full essay on the Substack, link in bio.

cards: Are you growing, or still trying to become acceptable?

GROWTH
A direction. You enjoy where you are while you move.

THE VERDICT
You're a draft. Enough is always one improvement away.
Seneca saw people forever changing plans and places. The restlessness came with them.
Idea: Seneca, On Tranquillity of Mind · Moodius words
Which one got you up this morning?
reels.caption:
Growth is a direction. Becoming, in the exhausting sense, is a verdict: who you are now isn't acceptable yet.

Seneca described people forever starting new plans, changing pursuits and places, and finding the restlessness came with them, because what they were escaping was themselves.

Which one is driving you?

Source: Seneca, On Tranquillity of Mind (paraphrased). Full essay on the Substack, link in bio.

carousel_caption:
There's a tiredness sleep doesn't fix: the tiredness of treating yourself as a permanent renovation.

Self-discrepancy research links the gap between who we are and who we should be to distress. A self that's never finished never closes it.

What could you declare finished this week?

Evidence: Higgins 1987 (theory; mixed support for specifics); WHO ICD-11; Curran & Hill 2019. Ideas: Byung-Chul Han; Seneca, On Tranquillity of Mind.
notes: Byung-Chul Han argues we've moved from a society that told us what we couldn't do to one that tells us we can do anything, so we must. The result isn't freedom but a new exhaustion: people who overwork themselves voluntarily, in the name of becoming.
A test for whether your self-improvement is growth or a verdict: if you stopped improving tomorrow, would you be allowed to rest? If the answer is no, the project has quietly changed what it's for.

Make a list of everything you're currently trying to improve about yourself. Most people find ten or more. Keep two. Write 'finished, for now' next to the rest. See which ones you actually miss in a month.
